social-contract: The social contract is the idea that political authority and the obligation to obey it rest on an agreement, real or hypothetical, among the people who are to be governed. It responds to the question of what could legitimately bind free individuals to a common power rather than leaving them in a lawless condition. Thomas Hobbes gave the theory its classic modern form, arguing that in a state of nature life would be one of perpetual insecurity, so rational individuals consent to surrender much of their freedom to a sovereign in exchange for peace and protection. Later thinkers such as Locke and Rousseau reworked the terms of the bargain, but the shared move is to ground the state in consent rather than in divine right or brute force.
rousseau-social-contract: The general will is Jean-Jacques Rousseau's term for the collective will of a political community aimed at the common good, as distinct from the mere sum of individuals' private interests. Rousseau argued that a legitimate state is one whose laws express this general will, so that in obeying them citizens are in effect obeying themselves and remain free even while bound. The idea addresses how a people can be governed without being subjected to any particular person's domination, locating sovereignty in the citizen body as a whole. It remains influential and controversial, since deciding what the general will actually requires, and who speaks for it, is far from straightforward.
rousseau-natural-goodness: This is Rousseau's claim that human beings are naturally good, or at least innocent, and that vice, inequality, and misery arise not from our nature but from the development of society and its institutions. In the imagined state of nature people are self-sufficient and compassionate, but the growth of property, comparison, and dependence corrupts them, breeding pride, envy, and injustice. The thesis reverses the older view that civilization tames a naturally wicked animal, and it frames Rousseau's political and educational projects as attempts to recover or protect that original goodness. It shaped Romanticism and modern debates about whether social conditions or human nature is the deeper source of our ills.
machiavelli-virtu: Virtù and fortuna are the paired concepts through which Niccolò Machiavelli analyzes political success and failure. Fortuna is the element of chance, circumstance, and shifting events that no ruler fully controls, while virtù is the skill, boldness, and adaptable resolve by which a leader seizes opportunities and imposes order on them. Machiavelli's point is not that outcomes are fated but that fortune governs perhaps half of what happens, leaving the rest to human effort, so the capable prince prepares against reversals and acts decisively when the moment allows. Virtù here is a hard-edged political competence rather than moral virtue in the Christian sense.
machiavelli-ends: The phrase 'the ends justify the means,' popularly associated with Machiavelli, expresses the view that in politics the rightness of an action can be measured by whether it secures a necessary and beneficial result, even when the action itself would ordinarily be condemned. Machiavelli argued that a ruler concerned with preserving the state may have to be prepared to act against conventional morality, using deception or cruelty when circumstances demand, because judging politics by private ethics alone can lead to ruin. He did not straightforwardly endorse wrongdoing for its own sake; his emphasis was on effective results and the harsh realities of power. The idea raises the enduring question of whether political necessity can ever license immoral conduct.
veil-of-ignorance: The veil of ignorance is a thought experiment devised by John Rawls to work out principles of justice that fair-minded people could accept. He asks us to imagine choosing the basic rules of society from an 'original position' in which we do not know our own place in it—our class, talents, race, gender, or conception of the good. Deprived of this knowledge, no one can tailor the rules to favor their own situation, so the principles chosen will be impartial and fair to all. Rawls argued that parties behind the veil would prudently choose principles protecting basic liberties and the worst-off, since anyone could turn out to be in that position.
justice-as-fairness: Justice as fairness is the name John Rawls gave to his theory of a just society, developed most fully in A Theory of Justice. Its core is that principles of justice are those that free and equal persons would agree to under fair conditions, modeled by the original position and the veil of ignorance. Rawls proposed two main principles: each person is guaranteed an extensive scheme of equal basic liberties, and social and economic inequalities are permissible only if they attach to positions open to all and work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged. The theory offered a systematic liberal alternative to utilitarianism and reshaped political philosophy in the late twentieth century.
difference-principle: The difference principle is the part of John Rawls's theory of justice that governs social and economic inequalities. It holds that such inequalities are just only insofar as they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society; otherwise a more equal distribution is required. The principle does not demand strict equality but permits differences in wealth and position when they raise the prospects of those at the bottom, for instance by providing incentives that increase overall resources. It reflects Rawls's conviction that the natural distribution of talents and starting points is morally arbitrary, so a fair society arranges its institutions to make the worst-off as well off as possible.
experience-machine: The experience machine is a thought experiment introduced by Robert Nozick to challenge hedonism, the view that pleasure or pleasant experience is all that ultimately matters. He asks us to suppose a machine that could give us any experiences we desired, indistinguishable from reality, for the rest of our lives, while our bodies floated in a tank. Nozick argues that most people would refuse to plug in permanently, revealing that we care about actually doing certain things, being certain kinds of people, and staying in contact with reality—not merely about how our lives feel from the inside. The example is a standard objection to purely experiential accounts of the good life.
minimal-state: The minimal state, or 'night-watchman state,' is Robert Nozick's ideal of a government limited to protecting people against force, theft, and fraud and to enforcing contracts. In Anarchy, State, and Utopia he argues that only such a state can be justified without violating individual rights, and that any more extensive state—one that redistributes wealth or imposes broader goals—wrongfully uses some people as means for others' ends. Nozick grounds this in an entitlement theory of justice, on which holdings are just if acquired and transferred through legitimate voluntary steps. His libertarian position stood as a direct rival to Rawls's more egalitarian liberalism.
communitarianism: Communitarianism is a strand of political philosophy that stresses the role of community, shared traditions, and social ties in shaping individuals and grounding moral and political life. It arose partly as a critique of liberal theories, associated with thinkers like Rawls, that picture people as freely choosing individuals abstracted from their attachments. Michael Sandel, a leading communitarian voice, argues that we are 'encumbered' selves constituted in part by loyalties and memberships we did not choose, and that justice cannot be defined independently of a community's shared understandings of the good. Communitarians therefore emphasize civic participation, common purposes, and the moral significance of belonging.
banality-of-evil: The banality of evil is a phrase coined by Hannah Arendt in her report on the trial of Adolf Eichmann, a Nazi administrator of the Holocaust. She used it to describe her impression that Eichmann was driven less by fanatical hatred or monstrous depth than by thoughtlessness, careerism, and an unreflective willingness to follow orders and cliché. The provocative claim is that immense evil can be carried out by ordinary people who fail to think about what they are doing, rather than only by demonic villains. Widely debated and often misunderstood, the idea directed attention to the moral dangers of unthinking obedience within bureaucratic systems.
arendt-totalitarianism: Totalitarianism, as analyzed by Hannah Arendt in The Origins of Totalitarianism, names a novel and radical form of domination exemplified by Nazi Germany and Stalinist Russia. Unlike ordinary tyranny, it seeks total control not just of politics but of every sphere of life, fusing ideology and terror to remould human beings and abolish spontaneity, plurality, and independent thought. Arendt traced its roots to phenomena such as antisemitism, imperialism, and the rise of atomized mass society, and argued that its concentration camps aimed to render people superfluous. Her account remains a landmark attempt to understand how such regimes arise and why they are distinct from earlier despotisms.
panopticon: The panopticon is an architectural design for a prison, conceived by Jeremy Bentham, in which a central watchtower can observe every cell while the inmates cannot tell whether they are being watched at any given moment. Michel Foucault took it up as a model for modern disciplinary power: because prisoners may always be under observation, they come to regulate their own behavior, so surveillance produces self-discipline without constant force. For Foucault the panopticon symbolizes how modern institutions—prisons, schools, hospitals, factories—shape docile, self-monitoring individuals. The image has become a touchstone in discussions of surveillance, control, and the effects of being perpetually watched.
power-knowledge: Power/knowledge is Michel Foucault's thesis that power and knowledge are not opposed but intimately bound together, each producing and reinforcing the other. Rather than treating knowledge as a neutral discovery of truth that stands apart from power, Foucault argues that systems of power generate the categories, institutions, and expertise through which certain claims count as knowledge, while knowledge in turn organizes and justifies the exercise of power. Fields such as medicine, psychiatry, and criminology, on this view, both study and help constitute their objects, defining what is normal, healthy, or deviant. The concept reframes truth as something produced within relations of power rather than existing prior to them.
